summary:
Diyarbakır is the largest city of Türkiye's south-east and stands under the national legal framework that Human Rights Watch and Kaos GL document as actively hostile to trans people. Official framing around "the family" and "public morals" is the stated basis of that policy, and enforcement has run ahead of legislation that remains unenacted.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years' imprisonment, permit charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony carrying up to four years, and, under civil-code article 40, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 together with a permanent-infertility mandate. Providers would face fines and up to seven years; patients up to three. Fifteen LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch has called for the draft's withdrawal. As of the reporting date the package had not been enacted, so it is not yet the law under which a visitor is charged, but it defines the direction of the regime.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, "A Major Siege", published 24 February 2026, records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total and predominantly detentions, 89 violations involving torture or ill-treatment against 51 the previous year, and six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected. The report describes hostility becoming explicit state policy under "Year of the Family" instructions. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these totals rest on media coverage and NGO monitoring and understate the underlying figure.

Diyarbakır is the site of the strongest anti-trans killing case in Türkiye's record. On 14 September 2024, the day of a national anti-LGBT "Great Family Gathering" rally, two men attacked two trans women with sharp objects in the Kayapınar district. Sudenaz Uran was killed at the scene and her friend was injured. The defendants recorded the killing and the recording entered the case file. On 19 December 2025 both were sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment for the intentional killing of a woman. During the trial the Family and Social Services Ministry's application to intervene was accepted while the local bar association's LGBTI+ commission's application was rejected, placing the state on record as guardian of "the family" and the victims' own representatives outside the courtroom.

That sentencing outcome cuts against the general pattern without displacing it. Six anti-LGBT deaths were recorded nationally in 2025 and only three were classified as hate killings, and the single strongest homicide-justice result produced anywhere in the country came from a court in this province, not from the national institutions.

Checkpoint identification is the routine exposure for a visitor. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. In the country's largest city in 2025 police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; one woman stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway. The source inventory supplies no equivalent checkpoint count for Diyarbakır, so the national identification rule and the capital's pattern are the operative warnings here.

Police presence in Diyarbakır is structurally elevated. The city carries a conflict-era security legacy of state-of-emergency legacies and the village-guard system, with high police density and detention powers held in routine use. Any stop, document check or GBT-style questioning in this setting should be treated as a documented identification event rather than a routine formality.

Placement of trans detainees follows registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near the national capital on 1 December 2025, and the case confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, including a trans man held in a women's prison. Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinated a demand for an independent investigation after other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Transition-related care is contracting. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. A trans patient in Diyarbakır can therefore expect medical records to carry a visible gender marker, and the draft package's proposed floor of 25 with an infertility mandate would narrow care further if enacted.
tangentialFactors:
Prison Insider's Türkiye profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, describes LGBT detainees held under segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement: arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Asymmetry between victim and accused is documented. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a sequence activists cite as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The Diyarbakır case is a comparison point rather than a norm. Where a district court delivered aggravated life imprisonment, capital-city enforcement in the same year produced street detentions, document checks and a court that admitted the state's family-ministry application while excluding the bar association's LGBTI+ commission.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Kaos GL's 2025 reporting is the primary quantitative record for residents: 313 right-to-liberty violations, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, six right-to-life violations and three classified hate killings, with trans people most affected, compiled without official statistics and therefore dependent on media monitoring.

Prison administration in Türkiye operates on registered sex for placement, and the Human Rights Association branches active in Diyarbakır, Izmir, Mersin and Aydın are part of the coordinated response demanding an independent investigation into the Sincan Women's Prison death of 1 December 2025.

The Family and Social Services Ministry intervened in the Kayapınar homicide trial on the state's side while the Diyarbakır bar association's LGBTI+ commission was refused admission, which defines the local litigation environment for LGBT people in the province.

The Health Ministry's September 2025 regulation removed the "other" option from hospital records and mandated e-reports, so residents in transition care face documentation that fixes a gender marker in official medical files.

Anti-LGBT mobilisation is organised at national level through state-sanctioned rallies such as the "Great Family Gathering", and the anniversary date of that rally coincided with the Kayapınar attack on 14 September 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the 11th Judicial Package remained a leaked draft at the time of reporting, with no enactment date sourced. Whether its provisions have been adopted, amended or dropped since is not established in the inventory.

Unresolved: the national sources on the draft law and on Kaos GL's 2025 violation counts record no province-specific enforcement or incidents for Diyarbakır. The Kayapınar killing and the December 2025 sentencing are the only Diyarbakır-level evidence supplied, and the province's exposure to GBT-style street stops is inferred from a capital-city pattern rather than counted locally.

Unresolved: whether the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that prompted the Health Ministry's September 2025 rule has any direct administrative application in Diyarbakır is not sourced; the regulation is national in reach but its provincial implementation is not documented here.

Unresolved: the outcome of the independent-investigation demand into the Sincan Women's Prison death of 1 December 2025, and whether any official was charged, is not established in the inventory.

Caveat: Kaos GL's 2025 figures rest on media coverage because Türkiye publishes no official hate-crime statistics, so the recorded totals understate the underlying incidence and cannot be treated as a complete count.

Caveat: Human Rights Watch's 2008 findings describe conditions before the legal changes made after 2018 and are historical context, not current law.
